# Leveraging Query Optimizers to Verify the Soundness of LLM-based Query Rewrites for Real-World Workloads, and More!

## Research question

An LLM rewrite may run faster and match one database’s results while changing the original SQL’s semantics.

## Method

QO-Verify generates optimizer memos and recursively searches for a common logical expression, matching operators, predicates and ordered children. A match implies equivalence under sound normalization and transformation rules; otherwise it returns Unknown. Search limits and missing rules reduce coverage.

## Evaluation

SQL Server experiments use four enterprise workloads described in the paper and TPC-DS, JOB and TPC-H, with tuned indexes. GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5 generate rewrites using four prompts and retries. Cold-run timings and equivalence checks are reported after filtering for identical current-database results.

## What the results support

The checker accepts approximately 37% of 3,100+ result-matching candidates. Acceptance ranges from 95% for hints to 8% for unconstrained rewrites. Median improvement for best verified rewrites is at most 6%, substantially below that for merely result-matching candidates. Default optimizer limits reduce overhead and coverage.

## Limits and qualifications

The soundness argument trusts optimizer rules and implementation; it is not a complete SQL decision procedure. Unknown candidates lack adjudicated equivalence labels. Workload totals conflict across the introduction and table. A displayed rewrite changes NULL handling relative to its accompanying rule. No public implementation or independent reproduction was verified.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

Adjacent support for preserving SQL semantics during agent refinement and for distinguishing proof, empirical result agreement and inconclusive checking. It does not assess natural-language intent, clarification or intrinsic unanswerability.

## Checks against the paper

These are interpretations checked against the source, not verbatim quotations attributed to its authors.

| QO-Verify is a complete semantic checker, and Unknown establishes inequivalence. | Sections 2–2.2 require a common logical expression reached through semantics-preserving normalization and optimizer transformations. Operator-specific matching includes predicates and ordered children. Missing transformation rules, heuristic guidance and search limits can prevent a match even for equivalent queries. The external result is True or Unknown, not a negative proof. | Sections 2–2.2, pages 2–5; Algorithm 1, page 4 | Treat positive verification as conditional on sound optimizer rules, applicable assumptions and correct matching. Unknown is inconclusive and is not an answerability or refusal label. The paper does not independently prove the entire SQL Server optimizer correct. |
| The reported 37% is recall over all truly equivalent rewrites, or demonstrates that remaining rewrites are wrong. | Section 4.2 discards approximately 32% of rewrites with differing results on the current database, ignoring row order, and calls the remaining 3,100+ rewrites candidates. Section 4.3 verifies 1,150+ of these, approximately 37%. It does not establish semantic equivalence or inequivalence for every Unknown pair. Prompt-specific acceptance is 95% for QHint, 24% for CTE, 20% for SubQ and 8% for General. | Section 4.2, page 8; Section 4.3 and Figures 12–13, page 10 | The observed statistic is acceptance among result-matching candidates, not equivalence recall or an overall error-detection rate.
